Hebrews 8:13 uses "old", "growing aged" and "near to vanishing" — the same ideas as Isaiah 51:6.
Matthew 9:16-17: new wine needs new wineskins.

Most commentators say Isaiah contrasts the temporary universe with God's eternal salvation: even creation will pass, but his saving work will not. They see Hebrews 8:13 as a separate point about the covenant, and think linking the two is a thematic echo, not an explanation.
Why does Jeremiah describe Judah's ruin as the earth becoming "formless and empty" (Jeremiah 4:23-26)?
Jeremiah uses the exact words of Genesis 1:2, tohu wabohu. The covenantal reading says Judah's fall in 586 BC was the undoing of God's covenant creation.

Jeremiah 4:22 says God's people are foolish and do not know him. Verse 23 says: I looked at the earth, and it was formless and void; at the heavens, and they had no light. Verses 24-26 add shaking mountains, no man, fled birds, and a fruitful land turned to desert. These lines run Genesis 1 backward: light, land, people, birds, fruitful land, all removed. The phrase "formless and void" (tohu wabohu) appears only here and in Genesis 1:2. On the covenantal reading, Jeremiah shows that the judgment of Judah was a "de-creation". The covenant world went back to chaos when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC.
Genesis 1:2 and Jeremiah 4:23 are the only two places with the full phrase tohu wabohu.
Babylon burned the temple in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:8-9). The sun did not go out, but Judah's world ended.

All major views accept the echo of Genesis 1 and agree the passage is about Judah's fall. Traditional readers say this shows how serious sin is, as if creation were undone, but not that Genesis 1 itself is about Israel.
Does the earth really mourn and the heavens turn black (Jeremiah 4:28)?
Not as feelings in soil or sky. The covenantal reading says it is God's people who mourn when he comes in judgment. The land and sky picture the nation and its leaders.

Jeremiah 4:27 says the whole land will be desolate, yet God will not make a full end. Verse 28 says that for this the earth will mourn and the heavens above be black, because God has spoken and will not turn back. The physical earth does not grieve. On the covenantal reading, the mourning belongs to the people of the land. Joel 1:10 says the ground mourns because the grain is ruined, but then calls the priests to mourn (1:13). Hosea 4:3 says the land mourns because of the people's sin. The darkened heavens picture the fall of the nation's rulers. So "earth" and "heavens" here are the covenant people, mourning under judgment.
Hosea 4:1-3: because there is no faithfulness in the land, the land mourns.
Lamentations 1:4: "the roads of Zion mourn" — the roads stand for the people who no longer travel to the feasts.

Others agree this is personification. But they say Scripture shows the land truly suffering from sin, through drought and ruin (Jeremiah 12:4), so "the earth mourns" describes real damage to the land as well as the people's grief.
Is Jeremiah 10:11-13 about the physical sky or about God's people?
Its plain subject is God as Maker of the real heavens and earth, against idols. One covenantal reading sees hints of Judah's coming trouble, but this passage is mainly about creation.

Jeremiah 10:11 says the gods who did not make the heavens and the earth will perish from the earth. Verses 12-13 say God made the earth by his power and stretched out the heavens by his wisdom. When he speaks, waters roar in the sky, clouds rise, and lightning and wind come. This is about real weather and real creation. One covenantal paper admits it is "difficult language" and links it to the calamity coming on God's people (10:17-22). A careful reading keeps both. The chapter does go on to Judah's exile. But verses 11-13 use "heaven and earth" in its physical sense, to show that the Lord, not the idols, rules the world.
Jeremiah 10:11 is in Aramaic, the language of the nations, so exiles could tell their captors.
Jeremiah 10:17-18 then warns: gather your bundle, for God will throw out the people of the land.

Traditional readers use this text as a clear case of "heaven and earth" meaning the physical creation. They see it as a control on figurative readings: the same prophet who used the phrase as a picture in chapter 4 used it plainly here.
Why do "the heavens and the earth and all that is in them" sing over Babylon's fall (Jeremiah 51:48)?
Because the oppressor of God's people is destroyed. The covenantal reading says those who sing are God's people and the freed nations.

Jeremiah 51:48 says the heavens and the earth and all in them will sing for joy over Babylon, because destroyers come against her from the north. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and the temple. Her fall meant freedom for the exiles (Jeremiah 51:45, 50). On the covenantal reading, the joyful heavens and earth are the people released from her power. Revelation 18:20 echoes this: "Rejoice over her, O heaven, you saints and apostles and prophets." There the word "heaven" is explained by "saints, apostles and prophets". The covenantal reading sees this as the Bible's own key to what a rejoicing "heaven" means.
Revelation 18:20 places "heaven" beside "saints and apostles and prophets" as those who rejoice.
Cyrus' decree (538 BC) let the Jewish exiles return home after Babylon fell (Ezra 1:1-4).

Most commentators see the line as poetic praise in which creation joins God's people. Some note Revelation 18:20 addresses heaven and then the saints as two groups called to rejoice, rather than defining heaven as the saints.
What does Hosea mean when God will "answer the heavens, and they will answer the earth" (Hosea 2:21-23)?

In the day God renews his marriage covenant, blessing flows from heaven to earth to grain and to "Jezreel", God's people. The covenantal reading sees heaven and earth tied closely to the covenant people.

Hosea 2:18 says God will make a covenant for his people with the animals, birds and creeping things, and break the bow and sword. Verses 19-20 say he will betroth Israel to himself forever in righteousness and faithfulness. Verses 21-22 say he will answer the heavens, the heavens will answer the earth, the earth will answer the grain, wine and oil, and they will answer Jezreel. Verse 23 says he will sow her in the land and call "Not my people" "my people". On the covenantal reading, heaven and earth here belong inside a covenant renewal. Paul and Peter apply Hosea 2:23 to the church of Jews and Gentiles (Romans 9:25-26; 1 Peter 2:10). The new heaven and earth is this renewed covenant people.
Romans 9:24-26: Paul applies Hosea's "not my people... my people" to Jews and Gentiles called by God.
1 Peter 2:10: once not a people, now God's people.

Others see a chain of blessing through real creation: rain from the sky, crops from the soil, food for the people. They say this shows covenant blessing reaching the physical world, which fits a renewed creation as well as a renewed people.
What were the "wonders in the heavens and in the earth" in Joel 2:30-31?
Peter said Joel's prophecy was being fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:16). The fulfilled reading places the wonders in the land of Israel between Pentecost and the "great day" of AD 70.

Joel 2:28-29 promises the Spirit on all flesh. Verses 30-31 add wonders in the heavens and earth, blood, fire and smoke, the sun dark and the moon blood, before the great day of the Lord. Verse 32 says those who call on the Lord will be saved. Peter quoted this whole text at Pentecost and said, "This is that" (Acts 2:16-21). The sun did not turn dark that morning. On the fulfilled reading, the whole passage covers one span: the gift of the Spirit, signs done by Christ and the apostles (Acts 2:22, 43), and the coming day of judgment on Jerusalem. Peter told his hearers to save themselves "from this crooked generation" (Acts 2:40).
Acts 2:16: "this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel" (KJV).
Darkness covered the land for three hours at the crucifixion (Luke 23:44-45), some weeks before Pentecost.

Many scholars see Pentecost as the start of Joel's fulfilment, with the cosmic signs either figurative or still future before Christ's return. Dispensationalists often hold that Joel will be fully fulfilled in the future tribulation, and that Pentecost was a partial fulfilment.
What does Habakkuk mean by "his glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise" (Habakkuk 3:3)?
Habakkuk recalls God coming from Teman and Paran, as at Sinai. The covenantal reading says praise comes from people, so the earth "full of praise" is God's people.

Habakkuk 3:3 says God came from Teman, the Holy One from Mount Paran. His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise. These places lie south, on the route of Israel's wilderness journey (Deuteronomy 33:2). The prayer recalls God's coming at Sinai and the exodus, then looks to future salvation (3:13). On the covenantal reading, who praises God but his people? Earth "full of praise" means a land filled with worshippers. Habakkuk 2:14 also promises that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of God's glory as the waters cover the sea. That is about people knowing God.
Deuteronomy 33:2: the Lord came from Sinai, rose from Seir, and shone from Mount Paran.
Habakkuk 2:14 echoes Isaiah 11:9: the earth full of the knowledge of the Lord.

Most commentators read this as a theophany: God's brightness fills the sky and his praise is heard across the world. They agree praise comes from people but read "earth" as the world in which they live.
What is the shaking of "the heavens and the earth" in Haggai 2:6-7 and Hebrews 12:26-28?

Hebrews says the shaking removes what can be shaken so that an unshakable kingdom remains. The fulfilled reading sees the old covenant order removed in the first century and the kingdom of Christ standing.

Haggai 2:6-7 says that "once more, in a little while" God will shake heaven, earth, sea and dry land, and all nations, and fill his house with glory. Hebrews 12:26-27 quotes this and says "once more" shows the removal of things that are shaken, so that what cannot be shaken may remain. Verse 28 says "we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken." The verb is present tense. On the fulfilled reading, the readers stood between Sinai and Zion (12:18-24). The thing being shaken and removed was the old covenant world. The kingdom being received was Christ's. John Owen and Milton Terry both linked this shaking with the fall of the Jewish state.
Hebrews 12:28: "we are receiving" (present tense) a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
Haggai spoke in 520 BC when the second temple was being built (Haggai 1:1; 2:3).

Many commentators read Hebrews 12:26-27 as the final shaking of the created order at Christ's return, after which only the eternal kingdom remains. Others see a two-stage fulfilment: Christ's first coming and AD 70 began it, and the final day completes it.
Why did God tell Zerubbabel, "I will shake the heavens and the earth" (Haggai 2:21-22)?
Because he would overthrow thrones and kingdoms. The text itself explains the shaking as the fall of nations' power, not of the physical sky.

Haggai 2:21 says to Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah, that God will shake the heavens and the earth. Verse 22 explains: he will overthrow the thrones of kingdoms, destroy the strength of the nations, and overturn chariots and riders. Verse 23 makes Zerubbabel, David's heir, like a signet ring. On the fulfilled reading, the shaking of heaven and earth is defined right there as political upheaval. Kingdoms fall, and David's line is kept. This prepares for Christ, son of Zerubbabel (Matthew 1:12-13), whose kingdom cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:28). Both Haggai texts use "heaven and earth" for world powers, not for stars.
Matthew 1:12-16 lists Zerubbabel in the line of Jesus.
After Haggai (520 BC), Persia fell to Alexander (331 BC), and his empire split among his generals.

Most scholars agree that the shaking here is political. They see it as part of God's rule in history and as pointing to the Messiah. Some still read Hebrews' use of Haggai as including a final cosmic shaking.
Why does Peter tell his readers to remember "the words spoken before by the holy prophets" (2 Peter 3:1-2)?

Because his hope of new heavens and a new earth came from the prophets, especially Isaiah. The fulfilled reading says Peter taught nothing new, so his words must be read in the prophets' covenant sense.

Peter says he writes to stir their minds to remember the prophets' words and the apostles' command (2 Peter 3:1-2). Paul said he taught nothing except what the prophets and Moses said would happen (Acts 26:22). Peter's readers knew the phrase "new heavens and new earth" from Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22. On the fulfilled reading, Peter directs them back to these texts on purpose. In Isaiah the new heavens and earth come with a new Jerusalem, a people who rejoice, and the judgment of rebels. So Peter's picture of fire and new creation should be read in the same way: the end of one covenant world and the full arrival of another.
Acts 26:22: Paul says he said nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses foretold.
Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 are the only Old Testament texts that say "new heavens and a new earth".

Others agree Peter draws on Isaiah but say that he, like Isaiah, describes a real renewal of the world. They note that later Jewish writings, such as 1 Enoch 91:16, also read Isaiah's promise as a cosmic renewal, which suggests Peter's readers could hear it that way.
Who were the mockers asking "Where is the promise of his coming?" (2 Peter 3:3-4)?
On the fulfilled reading, they were people in the 60s AD who saw the promised generation running out and doubted Jesus' word. The fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 answered them.

Peter says scoffers will come in the last days, asking where the promise of his coming is, since all things continue as they were (2 Peter 3:3-4). Jesus had said some standing with him would see him come in his kingdom (Matthew 16:27-28), and that this generation would see all these things (Matthew 24:34). The apostles taught his coming was near (Philippians 4:5; James 5:8; 1 John 2:18). On the fulfilled reading, by the mid-60s, over thirty years had passed. Some began to scoff. Peter answers that God is not slow (3:9). The mockers matched Jesus' servant who said, "My master delays" (Matthew 24:48). The events of AD 70 then silenced such doubts.
2 Peter was likely written about AD 64-68, before Peter's death under Nero.
James 5:8-9: "The coming of the Lord is at hand... the judge stands at the door."

Most interpreters say the mockers deny Christ's final return in any age, and that Peter's answer ("a day is like a thousand years", 3:8) explains a long delay. They see the scoffers' claim that "all things continue" as a denial of God's intervention in history generally.
Did the flood destroy the physical heavens (2 Peter 3:5-6)?
No. The sky and the planet remained after the flood. Peter says "the world that then was" perished. The covenantal reading concludes that the "heavens of old" were a people and their world-order.

Peter says that by God's word the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and by water. By these, "the world that then was" was flooded and perished (2 Peter 3:5-6). Whether the flood was global or regional, the sky was not destroyed. The same sun rose on Noah after the flood (Genesis 8:22). On the covenantal reading, what perished was people: the corrupt line described in Genesis 6:1-7. Peter uses "world" (kosmos) for the world of the ungodly (2 Peter 2:5). If the flood's "heavens and earth" can perish without the stars ending, then the coming fire on the present "heavens and earth" can do the same.
2 Peter 2:5: God did not spare "the world of the ungodly" (kosmos asebon) but saved Noah.
Genesis 8:22: after the flood God promises seedtime and harvest, day and night, will not cease.

Many commentators reply that the flood truly ruined the physical earth's surface and life, which is why Peter calls it destruction. They say Peter's point is that God has judged the physical world before and will do it again by fire, so the parallel supports a real cosmic event.
What are "the heavens and the earth which are now" (2 Peter 3:7)?
On the covenantal reading, they were the covenant world that began after the flood with Noah, ran through Abraham and Moses, and stood in Peter's day. It was "kept for fire".

Peter contrasts the world that perished in the flood with "the heavens and earth that now are", kept by the same word for fire on the day of judgment of ungodly people (2 Peter 3:7). God promised Noah he would not destroy the earth again by flood (Genesis 9:11). Through Shem and then Abraham the covenant line went on. At Sinai, God formed Israel as a nation. On the covenantal reading, this whole covenant order, centred finally on the temple, was the "heavens and earth which are now". It was reserved for judgment. The fire fell on that world when Jerusalem and the temple burned. The judgment Peter names is the destruction of "ungodly people", not of planets.
Genesis 9:11: God promises never again to destroy the earth with a flood.
Josephus describes the temple burning in AD 70, and the city later set on fire (Jewish War 6.4.5-7; 6.8.5).

Most readers see "the heavens and earth that now are" as the present physical world, which God will judge at the last day. They note Peter compares the flood with fire to show the scale of judgment, and that he expects ungodly people everywhere to face it, not only in Judea.
What "heavens" were judged by fire soon after Peter wrote?
On the fulfilled reading, the temple and Jerusalem, the centre of the old covenant world. Roman soldiers burned the temple in AD 70, within a few years of Peter's letter.

If Peter wrote about AD 64-68, the next great fire on God's people came very soon. The Roman general Titus took Jerusalem in AD 70. Josephus tells that a soldier threw a burning brand into the temple, and the fire spread through it (Jewish War 6.4.5). Later the Romans set fire to the city (6.8.5). The priesthood and sacrifices ended. On the fulfilled reading, this was the "fire" Peter warned of. Malachi had spoken of a day burning like an oven (Malachi 4:1). John the Baptist warned of chaff burned with fire (Matthew 3:12). Jesus told of a king who sent troops and burned their city (Matthew 22:7). Each points to AD 70.
Matthew 22:7: in the wedding parable, the king sends armies, destroys the murderers and burns their city.
Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5: the temple burned on the 10th of the month Lous (Ab), August AD 70.

Partial preterists such as Kenneth Gentry argue that 2 Peter 3 is the final consummation, not AD 70, because it speaks of the whole creation and of the destruction of ungodly people generally. Futurists and amillennialists agree. Some, such as John Owen, did read 2 Peter 3 as AD 70.
What are the "elements" that melt with fervent heat (2 Peter 3:10, 12)?

The Greek word stoicheia can mean physical elements, heavenly bodies, or basic principles. The fulfilled reading notes Paul uses it for the "elements" of the old law (Galatians 4:3, 9), and applies Peter's text to the old covenant order.

Peter says the elements will melt with burning heat (2 Peter 3:10, 12). The word stoicheia means the basic parts of something. In Greek writing it can mean earth, air, fire and water. It can also mean the heavenly bodies. In the New Testament it is used for basic principles: "the weak and beggarly elements" Paul's readers wanted to return to (Galatians 4:9), "the elements of the world" (Colossians 2:8, 20), and "the first principles of God's word" (Hebrews 5:12). On the fulfilled reading, Peter speaks of the old covenant's elements: its rituals, sacrifices and temple order. They "melted" in the fire of AD 70. Peter's readers had been warned not to cling to them.
Galatians 4:3, 9: Paul calls the old law's rules "elements" (stoicheia) that enslave.
Hebrews 5:12: "the first principles (stoicheia) of the oracles of God".

Most scholars say that in a passage about heavens, earth, fire and melting, stoicheia means the physical parts of the universe or the heavenly bodies, as in Isaiah 34:4 (Greek version). Richard Bauckham notes the word often meant heavenly bodies in this setting.
What does "the earth and the works in it will be burned up" mean (2 Peter 3:10)?
One covenantal reading sees the "works" as the works of the law and the temple that burned in AD 70. The oldest Greek copies read "will be found" or "laid bare", pointing to exposure in judgment.

The KJV says the earth and the works in it "shall be burned up" (2 Peter 3:10). The oldest manuscripts, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, read heurethesetai, "will be found". Many modern versions say "laid bare" or "exposed". This means all deeds will be uncovered before God. On one covenantal reading, the "works" are the works of the law that could not justify Israel (Galatians 2:16). When the temple burned, those works ended. A broader reading links "found" to Paul's picture of fire testing each person's work (1 Corinthians 3:13). Either way, the focus is God's judgment of human works, not the burning of rocks.
Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (4th century) read "will be found" in 2 Peter 3:10.
1 Corinthians 3:13: each person's work will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test it.

Most interpreters accept the reading "will be found" but apply it to the final judgment, when the earth and all deeds on it are exposed before God. They see "works" as all human deeds, not specifically the works of the Mosaic law.
What promise did Peter mean in "according to his promise we look for new heavens and a new earth" (2 Peter 3:13)?

The promise of Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22, the only Old Testament texts with that phrase. The fulfilled reading says Isaiah ties the new heavens and earth to a new Jerusalem and people, so Peter meant the new covenant world.

Peter says believers wait for new heavens and a new earth "according to his promise", in which righteousness lives (2 Peter 3:13). Most agree he points to Isaiah. Isaiah 65:17-18 says God will create new heavens and a new earth, and then explains: he creates Jerusalem as a joy and her people a delight. Isaiah 66:22 says that as the new heavens and earth remain, so will your seed and your name. On the fulfilled reading, Isaiah's new creation is a renewed people of God. That fits Peter's phrase "where righteousness dwells", because righteousness lives in people. Paul says believers in Christ are made "the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21). Peter waited for this new world to stand alone after the old was removed.
Isaiah 65:17-18 places "new heavens and new earth" next to "I create Jerusalem a rejoicing".
2 Corinthians 5:17-21: in Christ there is a new creation; we become the righteousness of God in him.

Most readers agree the promise is Isaiah 65-66. But they argue Isaiah pictures a renewed physical world and people together, and Peter, after a world-ending fire, expects a renewed cosmos. Gentry, Bauckham and Middleton all read 2 Peter 3:13 as the final new creation.
What were the "first heaven and the first earth" that passed away (Revelation 21:1)?
On the covenantal reading, the old covenant world: Israel's temple-centred order that began at Sinai, or, on a stronger form, began in Eden. It passed away in AD 70.

Revelation 21:1 says John saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and first earth had passed away, and there was no more sea. Isaiah 65:17 says the former things will not be remembered. The parallel is clear. On one covenantal reading, the "first" heaven and earth is the Mosaic covenant world, which Hebrews calls "the first" covenant (Hebrews 8:7, 13; 9:1, 8). On a stronger form, "first" points back to Genesis 1, read as the start of God's covenant people from Adam onward. Either way, John saw the old pass and the new city come. Revelation says its events were "soon" (Revelation 1:1, 3; 22:6, 10), which supports a first-century setting.
Hebrews 9:8: the way into the holy place was not yet open "while the first tabernacle was still standing".
Revelation 22:10: John is told not to seal the book, "for the time is at hand", unlike Daniel 12:4.

Most interpreters say the first heaven and earth is the present physical universe, which passes away or is renewed at Christ's return (Revelation 20:11). They see Revelation 20:11-15 (the final judgment) leading straight into chapter 21.
Does Scripture speak of any other creation of "the heavens and the earth" besides Genesis 1?

One covenantal paper says no, and so identifies the "first heaven and earth" with Genesis 1, read covenantally. Others point to Isaiah 51:16, where God "plants the heavens" at the exodus, as a second covenant creation.

Genesis 1:1 is the first creation of heaven and earth. One covenantal paper argues there is no other such creation in Scripture, so the "first heaven and earth" in Revelation 21:1 must be the Genesis creation, which it reads as a covenant creation of God's people. But other covenantal readers point to Isaiah 51:15-16, where God says he divided the sea and put his words in Zion's mouth "to plant the heavens and found the earth". This places a "creation" at the exodus and Sinai. Deuteronomy 32:6 also says God "made" and "established" Israel. On this view, the first heaven and earth of Revelation 21 is the Sinai covenant world, not Genesis 1.
Isaiah 51:16: God plants the heavens and founds the earth when he says to Zion, "You are my people."
Deuteronomy 32:6: "Is he not your father, who created you, who made you and established you?"

Traditional readers hold that Genesis 1 is the one physical creation, and Revelation 21 brings its renewal. They see the exodus language of "creating" Israel as figurative. Hence, they think the first heaven and earth must be the physical one.
Is the "new heavens and new earth" of Isaiah 65:17-19 and 66:22 about a covenant people?
On the covenantal reading, yes. Isaiah explains the new heavens and earth at once as a new Jerusalem and a joyful people, and promises "your seed and your name" will remain as they do.

Isaiah 65:17 says God creates new heavens and a new earth, and the former things will not be remembered. Verse 18 says: rejoice in what I create, for I create Jerusalem a joy and her people a gladness. Verse 19 says weeping will no longer be heard in her. Isaiah 66:22 says that as the new heavens and new earth remain before God, so will your offspring and your name. On the covenantal reading, the text defines its own terms. The new creation is a city and a people. It stands as long as God's people stand. The setting is covenant: God judges rebels (65:11-15) and blesses his servants. This is the glory of the new covenant, not a new solar system.
Isaiah 65:18: "I create Jerusalem a rejoicing, and her people a joy" (KJV).
Isaiah 66:22 links the lasting of the new heavens and earth with the lasting of Israel's seed and name.

Most commentators agree Isaiah focuses on a renewed Jerusalem and people. Many hold that the people and their world are renewed together, as in Isaiah 11:6-9 and 35:1-2. Premillennialists often see a millennial earth in 65:20-25, and the eternal state in Revelation 21.
What did Isaiah mean when he said God would slay the scorners and call his servants "by another name" (Isaiah 65:13-15)?
God would judge the rebels in Israel and give his faithful servants a new name. The fulfilled reading sees this in the parables of the vineyard and the wedding feast, and in the name "Christians".

Isaiah 65:13-14 contrasts God's servants, who eat, drink and rejoice, with the rebels, who are hungry, thirsty and ashamed. Verse 15 says the rebels will leave their name as a curse, the Lord God will put them to death, and he will call his servants by another name. On the fulfilled reading, Jesus told the same story. In the parable of the vineyard, the owner destroys the wicked tenants and gives the vineyard to others (Matthew 21:41, 43). In the wedding parable, the king burns the murderers' city and invites new guests (Matthew 22:7-10). The new name came too: "the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch" (Acts 11:26).
Acts 11:26 (about AD 40-44): the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch.
Matthew 21:43: the kingdom will be taken from you and given to a people producing its fruits.

Others agree Isaiah contrasts the faithful and the faithless within Israel. Many caution against reading Matthew 21:43 as God rejecting the Jewish people; the believing remnant was Jewish (Romans 11:1-5). Some see the "new name" as Revelation 2:17 and 3:12, given at the end.
Will the new heavens and new earth be a physical paradise with no death, pain or tears?

The covenantal reading says Isaiah 65 cannot be that, because death still happens in it (65:20). It reads the new creation as the new covenant life now, where spiritual death and condemnation are removed.

Many teach that God will remake the universe as a paradise with no death. But Isaiah's new heavens and earth still have death. A person who dies at a hundred is "a child" (Isaiah 65:20). A sinner is still cursed. People build and plant (65:21-22). Isaiah 66:24 even ends with the corpses of rebels outside the city. On the covenantal reading, this cannot describe a world with no death at all. It describes the new covenant age. In Christ there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Believers have passed from death to life (John 5:24). The tears and sorrow removed are the guilt and curse of the law. So the new creation is a present spiritual reality, growing in the world.
Isaiah 65:20: "the child shall die an hundred years old" (KJV) — death is still present.
Isaiah 66:24: those who worship look on the corpses of the rebels outside.

Premillennialists answer that Isaiah 65:20-25 describes the millennium, and Revelation 21 the eternal state. Amillennialists say Isaiah uses long life as a picture of perfect blessing, in the language his hearers knew. Both hold that Revelation 21:4 promises an end of physical death (1 Corinthians 15:26).
